title: Children sent by parcel post
hook: For a few years, some American parents sent their children by post.
peek: When the United States Post Office began carrying parcels in 1913, a handful of families realised that stamps could be cheaper than a train ticket. A small number of children travelled with the mail before officials put a firm stop to it.
lede: On 1 January 1913, the United States Post Office launched parcel post, letting people mail packages to rural homes for the first time. The rules said nothing clear about children. Within weeks, a few parents had tried it. The children travelled in the care of postal workers, often ones the family knew, and the practice lasted only a few years.

bullets.text: Early in 1913, a couple in Batavia, Ohio, handed their baby son to a rural mail carrier, who delivered him to his grandmother about a mile away. The postage was 15 cents, and the parents insured him for 50 dollars.

The best-known case came in 1914, when nearly six-year-old May Pierstorff was posted about 70 miles across Idaho to visit her grandparents. Stamps were attached to her coat, and she rode in the train's mail car with a relative who worked there.

The appeal was the price. Postage was charged by weight, and for a small child it could come to less than a train fare. The weight limit for parcels was raised during 1914, which brought more children within range.

Officials ruled that people did not count as mailable items, though a few more cases slipped through. By around 1915 the practice had ended. Photographs of children with mailbags, mostly staged for fun and now kept by the Smithsonian, keep the story alive.
